claim: High-content phenotypic screening has become the approach of choice for drug discovery due to its ability to extract drug-specific multi-layered data.
source: High-content phenotypic screening has become the approach of choice for drug discovery due to its ability to extract drug-specific multi-layered data.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field that draws from established scientific consensus about high-content screening methods.

claim: Epigenetic screening methods have suffered from a lack of tools sensitive to selective epigenetic perturbations.
source: In the field of epigenetics, such screening methods have suffered from a lack of tools sensitive to selective epigenetic perturbations.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the field based on the authors' assessment of existing methods.

claim: MIEL captures the nuclear staining patterns of epigenetic marks and employs machine learning to accurately distinguish between such patterns.
source: Here we describe a novel approach, Microscopic Imaging of Epigenetic Landscapes (MIEL), which captures the nuclear staining patterns of epigenetic marks and employs machine learning to accurately distinguish between such patterns.
evidence: This describes the methodology of MIEL as developed and tested in the manuscript.

claim: The MIEL platform was validated across multiple cell lines and using dose-response curves.
source: We validated the MIEL platform across multiple cells lines and using dose-response curves, to insure the fidelity and robustness of this approach for high content high throughput drug discovery.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental validation data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: MIEL can identify and classify epigenetically active drugs.
source: Focusing on noncytotoxic glioblastoma treatments, we demonstrated that MIEL can identify and classify epigenetically active drugs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing drug classification results.

claim: MIEL can accurately rank candidate drugs by their ability to produce desired epigenetic alterations consistent with increased sensitivity to chemotherapeutic agents.
source: Furthermore, we show MIEL was able to accurately rank candidate drugs by their ability to produce desired epigenetic alterations consistent with increased sensitivity to chemotherapeutic agents or with induction of glioblastoma differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing correlation between MIEL rankings and drug efficacy.

claim: The epigenetic landscape of a cell is largely determined by the organization of its chromatin and the pattern of DNA and histone modifications.
source: The epigenetic landscape of a cell is largely determined by the organization of its chromatin and the pattern of DNA and histone modifications. These confer differential accessibility to areas of the genome and through direct and in-direct regulation of all DNA-related processes, form the basis of the cellular phenotype (Jenuwein and Allis, 2001; Lawrence et al., 2016; Berger, 2007; Goldberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: ATAC-seq and histone ChIP-seq can be used to collect global information about the epigenetic landscape.
source: By collecting global information about the epigenetic landscape, for example using ATAC- or histone ChIP-seq, we can derive multilayered information regarding cellular states (Miyamoto et al., 2018; Mikkelsen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published methods.

claim: Current methods for collecting epigenetic information are not adapted for high-content drug screening.
source: However, current methods for collecting such information are not adapted for high-content drug screening.
evidence: This is an assessment of the field that motivates the development of MIEL.

claim: Novel image processing tools coupled with multiparametric analysis and machine learning have significantly impacted the ability to investigate and understand the output of phenotypic screens.
source: More recently, novel image processing tools coupled with multiparametric analysis and machine learning have significantly impacted our ability to investigate and understand the output of phenotypic screens (Kang et al., 2016; Scheeder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Phenotypic screening assays have not been adapted to extract and utilize information from the cellular epigenetic landscape.
source: Despite these advantages, such assays have not been adapted to extract and utilize information form the cellular epigenetic landscape.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the field that MIEL addresses.

claim: Malignant glioblastoma is the most common and lethal brain tumor.
source: While malignant glioblastoma is the most common and lethal brain tumor, current therapeutic options offer little prognostic improvement, so the median survival time has remained virtually unchanged for decades (Jhanwar-Uniyal et al., 2015; Parvez, 2008; Burger and Green, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Current therapeutic options for glioblastoma offer little prognostic improvement.
source: While malignant glioblastoma is the most common and lethal brain tumor, current therapeutic options offer little prognostic improvement, so the median survival time has remained virtually unchanged for decades (Jhanwar-Uniyal et al., 2015; Parvez, 2008; Burger and Green, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Tumor-propagating cells (TPCs) are a subpopulation of glioblastoma cells with increased tumorigenic capability.
source: Tumor-propagating cells (TPCs) are a subpopulation of glioblastoma cells with increased tumorigenic capability (Patel et al., 2014) operationally defined as early-passaged (<15) glioblastoma cells propagated in serum-free medium (Nakano et al., 2008).
evidence: This definition is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TPCs are more resistant to temozolomide (TMZ) and radiation therapy compared to the bulk of the tumor.
source: Compared to the bulk of the tumor, TPCs are more resistant to drugs, such as temozolomide (TMZ) and radiation therapy (Bao et al., 2006; Safa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The resistance of TPCs may explain the failure of traditional therapeutic strategies based on cytotoxic drugs targeting glioblastoma.
source: This resistance may explain the failure of traditional therapeutic strategies based on cytotoxic drugs targeting glioblastoma.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited resistance properties of TPCs.

claim: Targeting epigenetic enzymes can increase sensitivity to cytotoxic treatments in glioblastoma.
source: These include targeting epigenetic enzymes (i.e., enzymes that write, remove, or read DNA and histone modifications) to increase sensitivity to cytotoxic treatments (Jones et al., 2016; Strauss and Figg, 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Romani et al., 2018)
evidence: This approach is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Differentiating TPCs can reduce their tumorigenic potential.
source: and differentiating TPCs to reduce their tumorigenic potential (von Wangenheim and Peterson, 1998; Von Wangenheim and Peterson, 2001; von Wangenheim and Peterson, 2008; Lee et al., 2015; Song et al., 2016; Garros-Regulez et al., 2016).
evidence: This approach is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: MIEL profiles chromatin organization using the endogenous patterns of histone modifications present in all eukaryotic cells.
source: Here, we introduce Microscopic Imaging of the Epigenetic Landscape (MIEL), a novel high-content screening platform that profiles chromatin organization using the endogenous patterns of histone modifications present in all eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This describes the fundamental approach of MIEL as developed in the study.

claim: MIEL can classify epigenetically active compounds by molecular function.
source: We validate the platform across multiple cell lines and drug concentrations demonstrating its ability to classify epigenetically active compounds by molecular function, and its utility in identifying off-target drug effects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental validation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MIEL can identify off-target drug effects.
source: We validate the platform across multiple cell lines and drug concentrations demonstrating its ability to classify epigenetically active compounds by molecular function, and its utility in identifying off-target drug effects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data, such as the valproic acid example.

claim: MIEL utilizes four histone modifications: H3K27me3, H3K9me3, H3K27ac, and H3K4me1.
source: Primarily, we utilized four histone modifications: H3K27me3 and H3K9me3, which are associated with condensed (closed) facultative and constitutive heterochromatin, respectively; H3K27ac, associated with transcriptionally active (open) areas of chromatin, especially at promoter and enhancer regions; and H3K4me1, associated with enhancers and other chromatin regions (Figure 1a; Creyghton et al., 2010; Shlyueva et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the methodology and is supported by citations explaining the biological significance of these marks.

claim: H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 are associated with condensed facultative and constitutive heterochromatin, respectively.
source: Primarily, we utilized four histone modifications: H3K27me3 and H3K9me3, which are associated with condensed (closed) facultative and constitutive heterochromatin, respectively; H3K27ac, associated with transcriptionally active (open) areas of chromatin, especially at promoter and enhancer regions; and H3K4me1, associated with enhancers and other chromatin regions (Figure 1a; Creyghton et al., 2010; Shlyueva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone modifications supported by citations.

claim: H3K27ac is associated with transcriptionally active areas of chromatin, especially at promoter and enhancer regions.
source: Primarily, we utilized four histone modifications: H3K27me3 and H3K9me3, which are associated with condensed (closed) facultative and constitutive heterochromatin, respectively; H3K27ac, associated with transcriptionally active (open) areas of chromatin, especially at promoter and enhancer regions; and H3K4me1, associated with enhancers and other chromatin regions (Figure 1a; Creyghton et al., 2010; Shlyueva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone modifications supported by citations.

claim: H3K4me1 is associated with enhancers and other chromatin regions.
source: Primarily, we utilized four histone modifications: H3K27me3 and H3K9me3, which are associated with condensed (closed) facultative and constitutive heterochromatin, respectively; H3K27ac, associated with transcriptionally active (open) areas of chromatin, especially at promoter and enhancer regions; and H3K4me1, associated with enhancers and other chromatin regions (Figure 1a; Creyghton et al., 2010; Shlyueva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone modifications supported by citations.

claim: MIEL uses only texture-associated features for multivariate analysis.
source: To focus on the intrinsic pattern of epigenetic marks, we use only texture-associated features (e.g., Haralick's texture features [Haralick et al., 1973], threshold adjacency statistics, and radial features [Hamilton et al., 2007]) for multivariate analysis.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach with citations to the feature types used.

claim: Similar texture features have been successfully employed for cell painting techniques to classify subcellular localization of proteins.
source: Previous studies have successfully employed similar features for cell painting techniques combined with multiparametric analyses to accurately classify subcellular localization of proteins (Hamilton et al., 2007), cellular subpopulations (Loo et al., 2009), and drug mechanisms of action (Collins et al., 2015; Caie et al., 2010; Gustafsdottir et al., 2013; Loo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MIEL identified 122 compounds that induced significant epigenetic changes out of 222 tested compounds.
source: This analysis identified 122 compounds that induced significant epigenetic changes.
evidence: This is a direct result from the screening experiment.

claim: Active compounds were not uniformly distributed across all functional drug categories.
source: Active compounds were not uniformly distributed across all functional drug categories.
evidence: This observation is supported by the data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: Intensity-based thresholding identified 94 active compounds from the same library.
source: As a result, we identified 94 active compounds, which were distributed across functional categories similarly to MIEL-identified compounds (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct result from the comparative analysis.

claim: For each functional category, the number of compounds identified as active using thresholding was smaller than the number identified using MIEL.
source: For each functional category, the number of compounds identified as active using thresholding was smaller than the number identified using MIEL (Figure 1b) demonstrating MIEL's increased detection sensitivity over standard thresholding.
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: MIEL demonstrates increased detection sensitivity over standard thresholding methods.
source: For each functional category, the number of compounds identified as active using thresholding was smaller than the number identified using MIEL (Figure 1b) demonstrating MIEL's increased detection sensitivity over standard thresholding.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparative data.

claim: A single histone modification yielded similar detection rates to the combination of modifications across most functional categories using MIEL-based analysis.
source: Using MIEL-based analysis, a single modification yielded similar detection rates to the combination of modifications across most functional categories (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by data in the supplementary figure.

claim: Individual modifications using intensity-based analysis yielded lower detection rates compared to the combination of modifications.
source: Using intensity-based analysis, individual modifications yielded lower detection rates compared to the combination of modifications and displayed equal or reduced detection rates when compared to MIEL in all categories and modifications (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by data in the supplementary figure.

claim: Detection rates using H3K27me3 were consistently reduced across most active categories except for EZH1/2 inhibitors.
source: Of note, 3 of the four modifications used for MIEL analysis showed similar detection rates across most of the functional categories. However, detection rates using H3K27me3 were consistently reduced across most active categories (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a) except for EZH1/2 inhibitors, possibly due to the role these enzymes play in regulating this posttranslational modification.
evidence: This observation is supported by data and includes an inference about the mechanism.

claim: MIEL separated multiple categories of epigenetically active drugs with an average accuracy of 91.4%.
source: Results showed that MIEL separated multiple categories of epigenetically active drugs with an average accuracy of 91.4% (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis.

claim: Discriminant analysis utilizing intensity measurements from all four channels yielded only 51.6% average accuracy.
source: Although many of the epigenetically active compounds induced alterations in average fluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), a DA utilizing intensity measurements from all four channels was ineffective at separating the various categories and yielded only 51.6% average accuracy (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is a direct result from the comparative analysis.

claim: DAPI texture features yielded an overall classification accuracy of 65.6% compared with 86.4% provided by H3K9me3.
source: This yielded an overall classification accuracy of 65.6% (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b) compared with 86.4% provided by H3K9me3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is a direct result from the comparative analysis.

claim: DAPI and other DNA dyes may be an informative and cheap alternative to histone staining in some applications.
source: Despite reduced overall accuracy, it is evident that DAPI and other DNA dyes may be an informative and cheap alternative to histone staining in at least some applications when the analyzed epigenetic landscape are very distinct.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DAPI classification results.

claim: HDAC inhibitors targeting both Class I and HDAC6 displayed the same profile as Pan HDAC inhibitors.
source: HDAC inhibitors targeting both Class I and HDAC six displayed the same profile as Pan HDAC, and DA showed the two categories to be undistinguishable.
evidence: This is a result from the discriminant analysis.

claim: The similarity between Class I+HDAC6 and Pan HDAC profiles was likely due to the high expression of HDAC Class I and HDAC6 and low expression of other HDACs in the GBM2 glioblastoma line.
source: This was likely due to the high expression of HDAC Class I and HDAC six and low expression of other HDACs in the GBM2 glioblastoma line (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a,b,c).
evidence: This inference is supported by RNA sequencing data showing expression levels.

claim: Seven out of 85 compounds tested (8.2%) were identified as active but were misclassified by MIEL.
source: Of the 85 compounds tested, 7 (8.2%) were identified as active but were misclassified by MIEL.
evidence: This is a direct result from the classification analysis.

claim: Valproic acid is a commonly used anticonvulsant that also functions as a Pan HDAC inhibitor at high concentrations.
source: One of these was valproic acid, a commonly used anticonvulsant (Peterson and Naunton, 2005) which also functions as a Pan HDAC inhibitor at high concentrations (Phiel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Valproic acid induced detectable epigenetic changes even at low concentrations (<30 µM) after a short 24 hr treatment.
source: Though valproic acid is expected to inhibit HDACs only at high concentrations (>1.2 mM), a short 24 hr treatment induced detectable epigenetic changes even at low concentrations (<30 µM).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Low concentrations of valproic acid did not induce increases in histone acetylation or decreases in histone methylation similar to other Pan HDAC inhibitors.
source: However, when we quantified H3K27ac and H3K27me3 immunofluorescence intensity at these concentrations, no increase in histone acetylation or decrease in histone methylation similar to other Pan HDAC inhibitors (TSA, SAHA; Figure 1—figure supplement 5a) was seen.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data.

claim: Pan HDAC inhibitors TSA and SAHA induced similar transcriptomic changes that were not apparent in the transcriptomic profile of valproic acid-treated cells.
source: This analysis indicated that the Pan HDAC inhibitors induced similar transcriptomic changes that were not apparent in the transcriptomic profile of valproic acid-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: There is a high and significant correlation (R = 0.91, p<0.05) between MIEL-based distances and FPKM-based distances for drug-treated cells.
source: FPKM-based distances were then correlated to image texture feature-based distances, which yielded a high and significant correlation between these metrics (R = 0.91, pv <0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 5c).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from transcriptomic and MIEL data.

claim: MIEL can identify epigenetically active compounds and accurately categorize them according to their molecular mechanism of action.
source: Taken together, these demonstrate a unique ability of the MIEL approach to identify epigenetically active compounds, to accurately categorize them according to their molecular mechanism of action, and to detect off-target effects of compounds with known mechanism of action.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the collective experimental results.

claim: For most drug categories tested (inhibitors of Aurora, JAK, SIRT and EZH1/2), discriminant analysis yielded low average classification accuracies.
source: We found that for most drug categories tested (inhibitors of: Aurora, JAK, SIRT and EZH1/2), DA yielded low average classification accuracies (Figure 2a - Aurora kinase: 43.3%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a - EZH1/2: 62.5%, SIRT:4 6.2%, JAK: 37.2), indicating similar MIEL profiles across tested drug concentrations.
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis of concentration-dependent effects.

claim: Pan HDAC and HDAC Class I inhibitors displayed progressive profile changes allowing discriminant analysis to separate different concentrations at higher accuracy.
source: However, Pan HDAC and HDAC Class I inhibitors displayed progressive profile changes, allowing DA to separate the different concentrations at higher accuracy (Figure 2a – HDAC Pan: 80.9%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a - HDAC Class I: 82.2%).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis.

claim: Some compound classes, such as Aurora and JAK inhibitors, induce epigenetic alterations only in concentrations at which cell count is significantly reduced.
source: This demonstrated that some compound classes, such as Aurora and JAK inhibitors, induce epigenetic alterations only in concentrations at which cell count is significantly reduced, whether through toxicity or direct effect on proliferation (Figure 2b – dark blue and pink respectively)
evidence: This observation is supported by the correlation analysis of effect size and cell count.

claim: HDAC inhibitors have a concentration range where epigenetic alterations are not accompanied by reduced cell counts.
source: while other compounds, such as HDAC inhibitors, characteristically have a concentration range where epigenetic alterations are not accompanied by reduced cell counts (Figure 2b – green and yellow).
evidence: This observation is supported by the correlation analysis.

claim: SIRT and EZH1/2 inhibitors affected significant epigenetic changes without inducing significant changes in cell count.
source: Interestingly, both SIRT and EZH1/2 (Figure 2b – light-blue and red, respectively) inhibitors affected significant epigenetic changes without inducing significant changes in cell count.
evidence: This observation is supported by the correlation analysis.

claim: Low (0.1 µM) and high (10 µM) concentrations of HDAC inhibitors resulted in distinct and separable epigenetic landscapes.
source: In particular, our data suggest that low (0.1 µM) and high (10 µM) concentration of HDAC inhibitors resulted in distinct and separable epigenetic landscapes, suggesting potentially distinct chromatin/gene expression profiles and divergent biological outcomes when using a low vs high concentration of such compounds.
evidence: This is supported by the discriminant analysis results and includes an inference about biological implications.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between drug effect sizes across all 4 tested glioblastoma cell lines.
source: This revealed a significant positive correlation between all 4 cell lines pointing to similarities in their drug sensitivity profiles and demonstrating the robustness of the MIEL read out (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of effect sizes across cell lines.

claim: MIEL enabled accurate separation of cells treated with drugs modulating distinct functions, such as EZH1/2 or SIRT inhibitors with mean 100% accuracy.
source: This analysis enabled accurate separation of cells treated with drugs modulating distinct functions, such as EZH1/2 or SIRT inhibitors (5 and 3 compounds respectively; mean 100% accuracy; Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis across cell lines.

claim: MIEL was unable to separate drug subclasses with similar functions, such as class I and pan HDACs inhibitors with mean accuracy 76.8%.
source: However, we were unable to separate drug subclasses with similar functions, such as class I and pan HDACs inhibitors (6 and 17 compounds respectively; mean accuracy 76.8%; Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis.

claim: The magnitude of SIRT inhibition effect was significantly more effective in lines showing reduced Sirt1 expression.
source: For example, SIRT inhibition was significantly more effective in lines showing reduced Sirt1 expression (the main SIRT to deacetylate histone 3; n = 4 compounds, p<0.02; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c)
evidence: This correlation is supported by MIEL data and RNA sequencing data.

claim: There is a significant inverse correlation (R = −0.87) between Sirt1 expression and SIRT inhibitor effect size.
source: and there was a significant inverse correlation between Sirt1 expression and the effect size (R = −0.87; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from expression and MIEL data.

claim: The magnitude of drug induced profile changes varies between individual drugs within each drug class.
source: MIEL analysis indicated that the magnitude of drug induced profile changes, as measured by distance from DMSO replicates, varies between individual drugs within each drug class (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This observation is supported by MIEL distance measurements.

claim: Multiple PARP and BET inhibitors sensitized GBM2 cells to TMZ.
source: Though we did not identify any drugs that synergized (CDI < 0.7) with the radiation therapy (Figure 3b, right panel), multiple PARP and BET inhibitors (PARPi and BETi) sensitized cells to TMZ (Figure 3b, left panel).
evidence: This is a direct result from the synergy experiments.

claim: No drugs were identified that synergized with radiation therapy.
source: Though we did not identify any drugs that synergized (CDI < 0.7) with the radiation therapy (Figure 3b, right panel), multiple PARP and BET inhibitors (PARPi and BETi) sensitized cells to TMZ (Figure 3b, left panel).
evidence: This is a direct result from the synergy experiments.

claim: BET inhibitors increased TMZ effectiveness in three glioblastoma lines (454M, PBT24, and GBM2).
source: In three lines, BETi increased the TMZ effectiveness (average CDI: 454M 0.76 ± 0.28, PBT24 0.78 ± 0.12 and GBM2 0.51 ± 0.2; Mean ± SD; n = 11 BETi; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a direct result from the synergy experiments across multiple cell lines.

claim: BET inhibitors did not synergize with TMZ in three glioblastoma lines (SK262, 101A, and 217M) and were often protective.
source: In the other three lines, the drugs did not synergize and, in many cases, were found to be protective against (CDI > 1) TMZ (average CDI: SK262 1.4 ± 0.26, 101A 1.4 ± 0.22 and 217M 1.2 ± 0.21; Mean ± SD; n = 11 BETi; Figure 3c; p- values for all pairwise comparisons Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a direct result from the synergy experiments.

claim: Following a 6 days treatment, 6 out of 11 BET inhibitors induced significant epigenetic changes in all cell lines tested.
source: However, following a 6 days treatment 6 out of 11 BETi induced significant (average z-scored distance from DMSO replicates >3) epigenetic changes in all cell line tested (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a direct result from the extended treatment MIEL analysis.

claim: In lines displaying TMZ and BET inhibitor synergy, the degree of BET inhibitor activity significantly correlated with the degree of synergism.
source: In lines displaying TMZ and BETi synergy, the degree of BETi activity, as measured by MIEL, significantly correlated with the degree of synergism (Figure 3d – top panel).
evidence: This correlation is supported by MIEL and synergy data.

claim: MGMT provides the main line of defense against DNA alkylating agents such as TMZ.
source: O6-alkylguanine DNA alkyltransferase (MGMT), which provides the main line of defense against DNA alkylating agents such as TMZ, has been found to be epigenetically silenced through DNA methylation in a large fraction of glioblastoma tumors (Karayan-Tapon et al., 2010; Hegi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MGMT has been found to be epigenetically silenced through DNA methylation in a large fraction of glioblastoma tumors.
source: O6-alkylguanine DNA alkyltransferase (MGMT), which provides the main line of defense against DNA alkylating agents such as TMZ, has been found to be epigenetically silenced through DNA methylation in a large fraction of glioblastoma tumors (Karayan-Tapon et al., 2010; Hegi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All six tested glioblastoma lines expressed similar BET transcription factor levels such as Brd2.
source: This analysis showed that while all lines expressed similar BET transcription factors (TFs) levels, such as Brd2 (Figure 3e), and were thus susceptible to BET inhibitors, only the three lines displaying BETi-TMZ synergy expressed MGMT (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: Only the three glioblastoma lines displaying BET inhibitor-TMZ synergy expressed MGMT.
source: This analysis showed that while all lines expressed similar BET transcription factors (TFs) levels, such as Brd2 (Figure 3e), and were thus susceptible to BET inhibitors, only the three lines displaying BETi-TMZ synergy expressed MGMT (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: Treating glioblastoma lines with BET inhibitors dramatically reduced MGMT expression.
source: Treating those three lines with BETi, dramatically reduced MGMT expression (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data after BET inhibitor treatment.

claim: Combining BET inhibitors with the MGMT inhibitor Lomeguatrib did not increase sensitivity to TMZ above the levels conferred by Lomeguatrib alone.
source: Finally, combining BET inhibitors with the MGMT inhibitor Lomeguatrib did not increase sensitivity to TMZ above the levels conferred by Lomeguatrib alone (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is a direct result from the combination treatment experiments.

claim: Several BET inhibitors synergized with TMZ treatment by reducing MGMT expression.
source: In sum, we have discovered that several BETi synergized with TMZ treatment by reducing MGMT expression.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the collective experimental results on BET inhibitors, MGMT expression, and TMZ synergy.

claim: MIEL can rank BET inhibitors according to their magnitude of epigenetic effect, which correlates with their ability to synergize with TMZ.
source: We applied MIEL to rank BETi according to their magnitude of epigenetic effect and demonstrated that they ranks according their ability to synergize with TMZ suggesting that their mechanism of action involves epigenetic change.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between MIEL rankings and synergy data.

claim: The activity of PARP inhibitors didn't correlate with magnitude of epigenetic effect, suggesting an alternative mechanism of action.
source: In contrast, the activity of PARP inhibitors didn't correlate with magnitude of epigenetic effect, suggesting an alternative mechanism of action.
evidence: This is supported by the lack of correlation between MIEL measurements and PARP inhibitor activity.

claim: Fibroblasts, iPSCs, and NPCs each segregate to form three visually distinct territories on MIEL distance maps.
source: Multivariate centroids were calculated for each cell population and plotted on a distance map to visualize the relative Euclidean distance between various cell populations. The fibroblasts, iPSCs, and NPCs each segregate to form three visually distinct territories (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the distance map visualization.

claim: Discriminant analysis showed accurate separation of fibroblasts, iPSCs, and NPCs across all three donors with average accuracy 100%.
source: We separated the nine lines by cell-fates using DA, which showed an accurate separation of the different cell-fates across all three donors (average accuracy 100%; Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis.

claim: Discriminant analysis aimed at separating different donors showed only low accuracy (average accuracy 55.5%).
source: A similar analysis aimed at separate the different donors showed only low accuracy (average accuracy 55.5%; Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis.

claim: SVM classification indicated a high degree of separation between fibroblasts, iPSCs, and NPCs at a single cell level.
source: To determine whether it was possible to discriminate between individual cells with different fates, a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier was trained on a subset of fibroblasts, iPSCs, and NPCS from the three donors. Classification of the test set indicated a high degree of separation between the different fates at a single cell level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,d).
evidence: This is a direct result from the SVM classification.

claim: MIEL analysis using only H3K9me3 was able to discriminate between primary hematopoietic cell types freshly isolated from mouse bone marrow.
source: Additionally, MIEL analysis (using only H3K9me3) was able to discriminate between primary hematopoietic cell types freshly isolated from mouse bone marrow, namely lymphoid, myeloid, and stem/progenitors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the hematopoietic cell analysis data.

claim: Closely related hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells were not readily separated by MIEL.
source: However, closely related hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells were not readily separated (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the hematopoietic cell analysis.

claim: Discriminant analysis separated TPCs and DGCs with high accuracy (mean accuracy 100%).
source: Visualization using distance maps demonstrated that TPCs and DGCs segregate to form two visually distinct territories (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g) and were separated with high accuracy using DA (mean accuracy 100%; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis.

claim: SVM-based pairwise classification distinguished TPCs from their corresponding DGC lines with an average accuracy of 83%.
source: SVM-based pairwise classification of single cells distinguished TPCs from their corresponding DGC lines with an average accuracy of 83%, using any of the four epigenetic marks tested (H3K27me3, H3K9me3, H3K27ac, and H3K4me1; Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a direct result from the SVM classification.

claim: An SVM classifier derived from images of the MGG4 TPC/DGC pair separated all 3 TPC/DGC pairs with 88% average accuracy.
source: An SVM classifier derived from images of the MGG4 TPC/DGC pair separated all 3 TPC/DGC pairs with 88% average accuracy, providing proof of principle for the derivation of a signature for non-tumorigenic cells obtained following serum differentiation of primary glioblastoma cells (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is a direct result from the SVM classification and demonstrates generalizability.

claim: Three days of serum or Bmp4 treatment downregulated the four transcription factors Sox2, Sall2, Brn2 and Olig2 in a cell line-dependent manner.
source: Immunostaining revealed that the four transcription factors Sox2, Sall2, Brn2 and Olig2 were downregulated by both serum and Bmp4 in a cell line-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data.

claim: Three days of serum or Bmp4 treatment reduced expression of most genes constituting the transcriptomic stemness signature in GBM2 cells.
source: RNAseq analysis of serum- and Bmp4-treated GBM2 cells revealed that 3 days of treatment reduced (vs untreated cells) expression of most genes previously found to constitute the transcriptomic stemness signature (Patel et al., 2014) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Both serum and Bmp4 attenuated TPC growth rate.
source: Additionally, both serum and Bmp4 were found to attenuate TCP growth rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data.

claim: Expression of 4852 genes was significantly altered by either serum or Bmp4 treatment.
source: Expression of 4852 genes was significantly altered (p<0.01 and −1.5 < Fold Change>1.5) by either serum or Bmp4.
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of genes altered by serum or Bmp4 indicated enrichment in multiple GO categories consistent with initiation of TPC differentiation.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of these altered genes indicated enrichment in multiple GO categories consistent with initiation of TPC differentiation; these include cell cycle, cellular morphogenesis associated with differentiation, differentiation in neuronal lineages, histone modification, and chromatin organization (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Discriminant analysis allowed high accuracy separation of serum and Bmp4 treatments across all cell lines using both histone modification combinations (mean accuracy 100%).
source: Discriminant analysis allowed high accuracy separation of these treatments across all cell lines using both histone modification combinations (mean accuracy 100%; Figure 4h; Figure 4—figure supplement 5c).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis.

claim: There is a high correlation (Pearson correlation coefficient R = 0.93, p<0.001) between MIEL-based and global gene expression-based metrics for cellular states.
source: The resulting Pearson correlation coefficient of R = 0.93 (p<0.001) suggests a high correlation between these two metrics (Figure 4i,j), demonstrating that MIEL is capable of distinguishing closely related glioblastoma differentiation routes induced by serum or BMP and validating the robustness of the MIEL approach for analyzing glioblastoma differentiation.
evidence: This correlation is calculated from transcriptomic and MIEL data.

claim: MIEL analysis detected 144 active compounds from the Prestwick library screen.
source: This analysis detected 144 active compounds.
evidence: This is a direct result from the Prestwick library screening.

claim: 31 compounds from the Prestwick screen were classified as similar to either serum or Bmp4 treatment.
source: A total 31 compounds were classified as similar to either serum or Bmp4 (i.e., differentiated).
evidence: This is a direct result from the discriminant analysis classification.

claim: 20 out of 31 differentiation-inducing compounds belonged to one of four categories: Na/K-ATPase inhibitors, microtubule disruptors, topoisomerase inhibitors, or nucleotide analogues.
source: Of these, 20 compounds belonged to 1 of the following four categories: Na/K-ATPase inhibitors of the digoxin family, molecules that disrupt microtubule formation or stability, topoisomerase inhibitors, or nucleotide analogues that disrupt DNA synthesis (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a direct result from the classification and categorization of hits.

claim: There is a high degree of positive correlation (Pearson correlation coefficient R = 0.92, p<0.001) between MIEL-based and gene expression-based rankings of candidate drugs.
source: Comparison of the MIEL-based metric with the gene expression-based metric revealed a high degree of positive correlation between MIEL- and gene expression-based rankings (Pearson correlation coefficient R = 0.92, p<0.001; Figure 5c).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from transcriptomic and MIEL ranking data.

claim: Etoposide, the top MIEL-ranked candidate, altered expression of a large portion of genes in similar fashion to serum and BMP4.
source: To further visualize these results, we constructed heat maps depicting fold change in expression levels of genes associated with several GO terms enriched by serum and Bmp4. Our top candidate, etoposide, altered expression of a large portion of genes in similar fashion to that of serum and BMP4
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and heat map visualization.

claim: Digoxin, the lowest-ranking candidate, induced changes in gene expression that were rather different from serum and BMP4.
source: in contrast, the lowest-ranking candidate, digoxin, induced changes in gene expression, which were rather different from serum and BMP4 (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and heat map visualization.

claim: MIEL markedly improves detection of epigenetically active compounds compared to conventional intensity-based thresholding approaches.
source: Focusing on compounds that modulate epigenetic writers, erasers, and readers, we have shown that MIEL markedly improves detection compared to conventional intensity-based thresholding approaches and enables their function based categorization.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparative analysis of MIEL and intensity-based methods.

claim: MIEL readouts are coherent across multiple compound concentrations and cell lines.
source: We have demonstrated that MIEL readouts are coherent across multiple compound concentrations and cell lines and can provide information regarding drug activity levels and their mechanism of action.
evidence: This is supported by the concentration-response and multi-cell line validation experiments.

claim: A single histone modification was sufficient to separate highly distinct drug classes.
source: We found that a single histone modification was sufficient to separate highly distinct classes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the discriminant analysis using individual histone modifications.

claim: Separating similar drug classes required staining for at least one additional histone modification.
source: However, separating similar classes (e.g., Aurora and JAK inhibitors, which affect histone phosphorylation, or Pan and Class I HADCs, which affect histone acetylation) required staining for at least one additional histone modification (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by the discriminant analysis results.

claim: MIEL's ability to separate closely related functional categories makes it an attractive alternative for primary screens.
source: Consequently, MIEL's ability to separate closely related functional categories on top of other advantages make this profiling approach an attractive alternative for primary screens.
evidence: This is an inference based on the demonstrated capabilities of MIEL.

claim: Phenotypic profiling methods have been previously used to identify genotype-specific drug responses by comparing profiles across multiple isogenic lines.
source: Phenotypic profiling methods have been previously used to identify genotype‐specific drug responses by comparing profiles across multiple isogenic lines (Breinig et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MIEL could be used to identify cell lines showing an aberrant reaction to selected drugs and aid in identifying optimal treatments for individual patients.
source: Together, these suggest that MIEL could be used to identify cell lines showing an aberrant reaction to selected drugs and, therefore, aid in identifying optimal treatments for individual patients.
evidence: This is a speculative application based on the demonstrated coherence across cell lines and variation in drug responses.

claim: BET transcription factors bind elevated H3K27ac levels found in enhancers.
source: As BET transcription factors bind elevated H3K27ac levels found in enhancers (Sengupta et al., 2015; Lovén et al., 2013), this may suggest a possible mechanism for BETi-induced reduction of MGMT expression, which in turn results in increased sensitivity to the DNA alkylating agent TMZ.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Silencing the MGMT gene through promoter methylation increases responsiveness to TMZ treatment and improves prognosis in glioblastoma patients.
source: Silencing the MGMT gene through promoter methylation has long been known to increase responsiveness to TMZ treatment and improve prognosis in patients with glioblastoma (Karayan-Tapon et al., 2010; Hegi et al., 2005; Esteller et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Clinical trials combining TMZ and MGMT inhibitors have not improved therapeutic outcomes in glioblastoma patients.
source: Yet Despite that, clinical trials that combine TMZ and MGMT inhibitors have not improved therapeutic outcomes in such patients, possibly due to the 50% reduction in dose of TMZ, which is required to avoid hematologic toxicity (Quinn et al., 2009a; Quinn et al., 2009b; Quinn et al., 2009c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial results.

claim: BET inhibitors offer an attractive line of research for improving glioblastoma treatment.
source: Thus, BETi offers an attractive line of research, though further studies are needed to determine whether the elevated sensitivity of glioblastoma to BETi, and its ability to reduce MGMT expression could be exploited to improve patient outcome.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings about BET inhibitors and MGMT.

claim: Serum and BMP4 are two established biologicals known to induce glioblastoma differentiation in culture.
source: We analyzed serum and BMP4, two established biologicals known to induce glioblastoma differentiation in culture (Lee et al., 2006; Piccirillo et al., 2006; Pollard et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: This is the first time that a signature for glioblastoma differentiation suitable for high-throughput drug screening has been obtained.
source: This is the first time that a signature for glioblastoma differentiation suitable for high-throughput drug screening has been obtained.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach.

claim: Results of previous studies using bulk glioblastoma analysis or single-cell sequencing could not be readily applied for high-throughput screening.
source: Indeed, results of previous studies using bulk glioblastoma analysis (Carén et al., 2015) or single-cell sequencing (Patel et al., 2014) could not be readily applied for high-throughput screening.
evidence: This is an assessment of previous methods with citations.

claim: The degree of reduction in endogenous SOX2 protein levels following drug treatment did not correlate with the degree of differentiation assessed by global gene expression.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that the degree of reduction in endogenous SOX2 protein levels following drug treatment did not correlate with the degree of differentiation assessed by global gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2d); in contrast, MIEL-based metrics did correlate.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis comparing Sox2 levels and transcriptomic profiles.

claim: MIEL can serve as a cost-effective tool for prioritizing compounds during primary screenings.
source: This result, taken together with MIEL's ability to distinguish multiple cells types (iPSCs, NPCs, fibroblasts, hematopoietic lineages; Figure 4b,c; Figure 4—figure supplement 2) across several genetic backgrounds, demonstate that the MIEL approach can readily identify compounds inducing desired changes in cell fate and that it can serve as a cost-effective tool for prioritizing compounds during the primary screenings.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the collective results demonstrating MIEL's capabilities.
